tags.gist: Says most health systems cannot reliably observe deployed devices, cannot list their AI-enabled functions, and cannot record which model version produced an output.
Recommends that institutions be asked to receive information and report, not to evaluate devices independently.
Recommends master files with a public tier instead of a wholly confidential structure.
Argues that if postmarket monitoring depends on institutions, it should be designed around what they can actually do, since most cannot observe devices reliably.
Explains that software devices enter through other procurement channels and seldom reach the item master, so many institutions cannot list or monitor them.
Warns that re-benchmarking, sample review and drift monitoring need the version, prompt and guardrails behind each output, which most institutions cannot record.
Notes institutions have no pathway for learning of third-party model changes, and asks any monitoring role to specify what information they receive and when.
Warns that monitoring capability is uneven across health systems, and asks CDRH to weigh resting the monitoring burden more heavily on manufacturers.
Reports that public FDA device data let the commenter and other researchers do independent postmarket risk analysis without proprietary manufacturer data.
Proposes a narrow public tier of master files, such as authorized versions and change dates, while weighing the risk to voluntary participation.
Lists three realistic institutional contributions, all dependent on manufacturer-supplied information, so accountability stays with manufacturers and evaluation is not expected of institutions.
Summarizes recommendations: institutions receive and report rather than evaluate, and FDA specifies what manufacturers must supply them, such as version identifiers and change notices.
Summarizes the recommendation of a tiered master file with a defined public subset and confidential competitively sensitive content.
Concludes that the postmarket approach presumes an institutional observation capability most health systems lack, and should be designed around that reality.
